title: Invisible nudges, new label
hook: Change every pixel by 1%, too little to see. Can the model's answer change?

knows: that a classifier turns an input into a label
that a decision has a threshold or boundary
doesNotKnow: why a barely changed input can flip a label
that many tiny changes add up across many inputs

misconception: Changes too small to see cannot change a model's answer.
objective: The learner can explain that a model that adds up many inputs can be pushed across its threshold by a tiny change to each one, and that the more inputs there are, the smaller each change needs to be.

claims.text: The toy classifier adds 100 pixel values (each weight 1) and says 'cat' if the sum is above 50. The toy image sums to 50.5.
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (N, START_SUM, THRESHOLD, makeImage). The grey pattern comes from mulberry32 seed 7 (untuned; it only sets the shades, the sum is fixed to 50.5 by construction).

claims.text: Darkening all 100 pixels by 0.01 lowers the sum by 100 × 0.01 = 1.0, twice the 0.5 margin, to 49.5, which is not above 50, so the label flips to 'not cat'.
claims.source: Arithmetic; reproduced by sumAfter(100, 10) = 49500 thousandths in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: With all 100 pixels a nudge of 0.005 (0.5%) each is already enough (sum exactly 50.0, not above 50); with 50 pixels it takes 0.01 (1%) each.
claims.source: The flip needs count × eps ≥ 0.5: eps = 0.5 / 100 = 0.005 and 0.5 / 50 = 0.01. Reproduced by sumAfter(100, 5) = 50000 and sumAfter(50, 10) = 50000 in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: A 1% change is about 2.5 grey levels out of 255, hard to spot by eye.
claims.source: 0.01 × 255 = 2.55 (arithmetic). On visibility: Goodfellow, Shlens & Szegedy 2015 (ICLR, arXiv:1412.6572) describe a perturbation of 0.007, the size of the smallest bit of an 8-bit image, as imperceptible. The perceptual claim is about humans in general, not measured here.

claims.text: A 224 × 224 colour image has 150,528 inputs; a margin of 0.5 spread over them needs about 0.000003 per input.
claims.source: 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528; 0.5 / 150,528 = 3.3 × 10⁻⁶. Applies to the toy's weight-1 adding rule, not to any particular real model.

claims.text: Real image classifiers have been fooled by changes too small to see, and the adding-up of many small changes across many inputs is one explanation offered.
claims.source: About real systems, from papers: Szegedy et al. 2014, 'Intriguing properties of neural networks' (ICLR, arXiv:1312.6199); Goodfellow, Shlens & Szegedy 2015, 'Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples' (ICLR, arXiv:1412.6572), the linear explanation.

recall.question: A spam filter adds up small scores for hundreds of words. A spammer swaps many words for near-synonyms, each worth a tiny bit less. Can this get the email through?
options: Yes: many tiny drops can add up past the threshold
No: each change is too small to matter
Only if one swapped word is a strong spam signal
recall.why: A model that sums many inputs responds to the total change. Small changes in many places add up, so no single change needs to be noticeable.
